column6: The commentary makes yawm al-din a day of reckoning under the sovereign; Daniel's Aramaic court sits and books open for judgment, adding an apocalyptic courtroom with deeds recorded.

column5: no human ransom for a life

column5: two ways of life and death
column6: The commentary prays for the path of the graced and distinguishes it from the astray; the Didache opens by naming two ways, one of life and one of death, giving an early Christian ethical frame for that choice.

column5: those in tombs hear the voice
column6: The commentary's standing scene presupposes the dead are raised; Jesus says all in the tombs will hear his voice, adding a summons from the life-giving judge.

The commentary separates the guided from the astray under final judgment; John says those who did good come out to resurrection of life and those who did evil to resurrection of judgment, giving an explicit two-outcome scene.
The commentary has creation stand before the one who sustains all; Paul says all will stand before God's judgment seat, making universal accountability explicit.

column5: day of wrath; who can stand?
column6: The commentary glosses divine anger as punishment and links q-w-m to standing; Revelation's terrified rulers ask who can stand on the great day of wrath, joining both details in one scene.

column5: day of wrath and righteous judgment
column6: The commentary treats the day as a certain reckoning and Allah's anger as punishment; Paul names a day of wrath when God's righteous judgment is revealed, supplying a close Christian formulation.
The commentary glosses din as account and recompense; Paul says God will repay each according to works, giving the day’s balance a direct ethical rule.
The commentary explains dīn as recompense and equal payment; the psalm says the Lord repays each person according to his deed, matching that account-and-return sense.
The commentary says no one disappears from the day's account; Proverbs says the one who weighs hearts knows and repays each according to his work, joining hidden knowledge with recompense.

The commentary notes the witness whose memory may fail and the blood that can be lost unavenged; after exposing false measures Amos swears God will never forget their deeds, making divine memory answer human evasion.

column5: the approaching day of the Lord
column6: The commentary presents yawm as a severe event that arrives; Zephaniah calls the great day of the Lord near and hastening, adding a prophetic day-of-judgment formula.
The commentary reads divine anger as punitive retribution; Zephaniah describes the day as wrath, distress and ruin, specifying the judgment's felt consequence.

The commentary distinguishes the graced from the angered and astray; Jesus gathers all nations before the enthroned Son of Man and separates people as a shepherd separates sheep and goats, making the division a judgment scene.

The commentary contrasts those under anger with those guided on the favored path; Jesus' judgment ends in eternal punishment for one group and eternal life for the other, giving the separation its final stakes.
The commentary connects the straight-path root label to resurrection and standing; 4 Ezra says earth and dust will restore those sleeping in them, adding a detailed restoration scene before judgment.

column5: Most High revealed at judgment seat
column6: The commentary presents the day as the sovereign's account; 4 Ezra says the Most High is revealed at the judgment seat, while compassion and patience withdraw, giving the scene an explicitly judicial climax.

The commentary defines the malik branch as one with command and authority; Wisdom says rulers received sovereignty from God, who will examine their works, making earthly rule answerable to the final sovereign.

column5: kings stand before the enthroned one
column6: The commentary places humanity standing before the life-sustainer on the day of account; 1 Enoch says kings and mighty ones stand before the enthroned Elect One, extending the reckoning to earthly rulers.

The commentary develops the exact balance and full-weight coin as an image of judgment; the Testament depicts deeds weighed for a soul, adding a Jewish apocalyptic scene in which moral outcome is literally assessed on scales.

The source commentary explicitly labels ٱلدِّينِ and glosses it as ḥisāb and recompense; Daniel's Aramaic דִּינָא names the court/judgment as it sits. This is a judicial cognate, while the commentary still distinguishes Arabic dīn from deyn debt.
The source labels مَٰلِكِ with root م ل ك and describes its royal command; Isaiah calls YHWH judge, lawgiver and “our king” in one verse, showing the cognate royal term in a judicial setting.

column5: Hebrew יום יהוה, “day of the Lord”
column6: The source commentary labels يَوْمِ and develops it as an arriving judgment event; Zephaniah uses the cognate Hebrew יוֹם in its approaching “day of the Lord,” placing the judgment in a shared Semitic day formula.

The source labels ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ with root ق و م and explicitly connects that family to rising; Psalm 1 uses Hebrew יָקֻמוּ for the wicked not standing in judgment, a cognate standing sense rather than a claim that both words mean “straight.”
The commentary makes the upright path a balance that does not lean; Leviticus commands honest scales, stones and measures, grounding the image in Israel's market law.
The commentary imagines the final measure as a perfectly straight scale; Proverbs says honest balances and weights belong to the Lord, linking fairness in commerce to divine authority.
The commentary's “standing” coin has exact weight and does not tip the scale; Deuteronomy requires a full and just weight, making commercial accuracy a covenant obligation.

The commentary describes a day when deeds are accounted and outcomes differ; the Talmud says books are opened on Rosh Hashanah and distinguishes righteous, wicked and intermediate people, adding a Jewish liturgical calendar for judgment.

column5: account on the day of judgment
column6: The commentary makes dīn an account and repayment; Jesus says people will give an account for careless words on the day of judgment, extending the reckoning to speech.

The commentary says no equivalent can be offered on that day; Jesus asks what a person could give in exchange for life after gaining the world and losing himself, sharpening the limit on substitution.

The commentary distinguishes a due debt from its final repayment; Jesus tells of two debtors unable to repay whom one creditor freely forgives, showing debt as a measure of mercy as well as liability.

The commentary distinguishes the source word dīn from the related deyn debt; Jesus' prayer asks forgiveness of sins while naming those indebted to the speakers, explicitly joining moral fault to debt language.

column5: release of debts in the seventh year
column6: The commentary uses a loan due at its term to illuminate the final account; Deuteronomy commands creditors to release claims at the sabbatical year, adding a Torah practice of debt remission rather than final collection.
The commentary frames judgment as an individual account; Paul says each person will give an account of himself to God, making responsibility personal rather than transferable.

column5: account before judge of living and dead
column6: The commentary's day leaves no one absent from the account; Peter says people will give account to the one ready to judge the living and the dead, tying accountability to the whole human span.
The commentary glosses din as recompense and anger as punishment; Paul says God repays affliction to those who afflict, making retribution a balancing of harms.
The commentary interprets divine anger as punitive consequence; Paul describes punishment when the Lord Jesus is revealed, placing that consequence at an eschatological appearance.

column5: judgment on wage fraud and perjury
column6: The commentary joins divine judgment with crooked weighing and a witness who might fail; Malachi says God comes near to judge those who oppress wage-earners and swear falsely, making economic and testimonial injustice explicit charges.

The commentary's branch gloss says blood can go to waste if vengeance is not taken; God tells Cain Abel's blood cries from the ground, a contrary image in which murdered blood remains heard even before human vengeance.

The commentary's qisas branch describes a life claim that can be converted to blood-price; Deuteronomy states life for life and forbids pity, supplying the retributive baseline that makes the conversion a meaningful difference.

column5: no payment to return from refuge
column6: The commentary develops substitute payment and blood-price as possible exchanges; Numbers also bars a ransom for a killer to return from refuge before the high priest's death, specifying a second boundary on monetary substitution.

The commentary says a person's offered equivalent cannot settle the final account; Peter says believers were ransomed from futile inherited conduct not with silver or gold, giving a Christian account of redemption whose means differs from a cash equivalent.

The commentary says the balance is not tilted by a substitute offered on judgment day; Peter identifies Christ's precious blood as the ransom price, a Christian atonement reading that locates redemption in another's life rather than the debtor's payment.

The commentary glosses divine anger as punishment and says no counter-value is accepted that day; Paul says people justified by Christ's blood will be saved from wrath, a distinct Christian account of how judgment is escaped.
The commentary makes the day of account universal and unavoidable; Hebrews says people die once and after that comes judgment, adding a concise sequence of death and reckoning.

column5: Christ bears sins; appears to save
column6: The commentary says no offered substitute is accepted on the judgment day; Hebrews says Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many and will appear to save those awaiting him, setting out a Christian mediating account while placing the offering before the second appearance.

column5: buy truth; do not sell it
column6: The commentary depicts guidance and error as the two sides of a bad trade; Proverbs says to buy truth and not sell it, treating moral knowledge as something whose value must be guarded.

column5: exchange glory for what is worthless
column6: The commentary's source gloss makes guidance and misguidance opposite sides of a failed purchase; Jeremiah says Israel exchanged its glory for what does not profit, giving the bad exchange a covenantal setting.
The commentary describes hidaya and dalala as a failed trade; Paul says people exchanged God's truth for a lie and worshiped the creature, applying exchange language to misdirected worship.

The commentary asks for the straight path and marks out the astray; Jesus contrasts a wide gate and broad way leading to destruction with the narrow way, making moral direction a choice of route and destination.

column5: Isaiah's straight way applied to John
column6: The commentary's prayer is for guidance on a straight path; John identifies the wilderness voice with Isaiah's call to make the Lord's way straight, interpreting the path as preparation for the Lord's arrival through John the Baptist.

The commentary brings a deferred debt into the judgment image; Deuteronomy announces remission at the end of every seven years, supplying the legal timing and social practice behind a debt's due term.

column5: erring from the way of truth
column6: The commentary distinguishes the favored path from those who stray; the wicked in Wisdom's postmortem confession say they wandered from the way of truth, adding a scene where the astray recognize their error after the righteous are vindicated.
The commentary contrasts a straight path with misguidance; the same confession says the wicked wearied themselves on paths of lawlessness, making the failed route a life of chosen conduct.

The commentary links q-w-m with the resurrection before the Sustainer; the tortured martyr says the King of the world will raise those who die for his laws, adding a Jewish resurrection hope grounded in fidelity.

The source commentary labels ٱلدِّينِ and explicitly glosses it as judgment/account; Moses' song uses the Hebrew d-y-n cognate when YHWH judges his people, supporting the judicial sense without equating the Arabic word's full range.
